chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Abi Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

He said: Indeed, Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, did not create anything except that He intended it to be worshipped, and He did not create anything except that He intended it to be a means of drawing near to Him, and He did not create anything except that He intended its knowledge to be learned, and He did not create anything except that He intended it to be a source of blessing.

So Salat is worship, Zakat is worship, Sawm is worship, Hajj is worship, Jihad is worship, the Book is knowledge, Amanah (trust) is knowledge, Sadaqah (charity) is a means of nearness, Ihsan (goodness) is a means of nearness, Sabr (patience) is a means of nearness, Shukr (gratitude) is a means of nearness, Rida (contentment) is a means of nearness, Khawf (fear) is a means of nearness, Raja' (hope) is a means of nearness, Himma (ambition/effort) is a means of nearness, Ikhlas (sincerity) is a means of nearness, Sidq (truthfulness) is a means of nearness, Sabr upon the disliked is a means of nearness, and Sabr upon the beloved is a means of nearness.
He said: So everything from the creation of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, is intended by Him to be worshipped, or a means of nearness, or its knowledge to be learned, or a source of blessing.

key_terms.تَبَرُّكٌ: Blessing (seeking spiritual benefit from created things)
key_terms.تَقَرُّبٌ: Drawing near (to God through virtuous acts)
key_terms.عِلْمٌ: Knowledge (specifically divine knowledge to be acquired)

ai.seo_question: What are the four purposes of creation according to Imam al-Sadiq in this hadith?
ai.summary: In *Kamal al-Din*, Shaykh al-Saduq records Imam al-Sadiq’s (a) elucidation that divine creation is structured around four primary intents: worship (*ibadah*), nearness (*taqarrub*), knowledge (*ilm*), and blessing (*tabarruk*). This classification distinguishes obligatory acts like prayer from spiritual virtues such as patience, highlighting the Shia emphasis on both ritual compliance and inner moral refinement as pathways to divine proximity.
